reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: EGPA is an eosinophil-rich, often ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that almost always arises on a background of adult-onset, frequently difficult-to-control asthma

The illness classically evolves through phases: an allergic phase with asthma and rhinosinusitis, an eosinophilic phase with blood and tissue eosinophilia, and a vasculitic phase with systemic involvement
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is a hallmark, and its degree helps distinguish EGPA from other ANCA-associated vasculitides
Neurologic involvement, especially mononeuritis multiplex causing asymmetric sensorimotor deficits, is a characteristic and clinically important feature
Cardiac involvement-myocarditis, heart failure, and coronary or pericardial disease-is a leading cause of death and mandates cardiac assessment even when asymptomatic

ANCA (usually anti-MPO/p-ANCA) is positive in a minority; ANCA-positive disease tends toward vasculitic manifestations such as neuropathy and glomerulonephritis, while ANCA-negative disease more often shows cardiac and lung involvement
Diagnosis integrates the clinical picture with eosinophilia and, where feasible, biopsy showing eosinophilic tissue infiltration, extravascular granulomas, and necrotising vasculitis

Corticosteroids are the foundation of treatment, with additional immunosuppression for organ-threatening disease and anti-IL-5 (eosinophil-directed) biologic therapy used to control eosinophilic disease and spare steroids
A recognised though debated association exists between leukotriene-receptor antagonists and unmasking of EGPA, often linked to reduction of background corticosteroids
reference.pathophysiology: EGPA is a systemic disorder combining marked eosinophilia with small- and medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis and extravascular eosinophilic granulomas. Th2-driven immune responses with elevated interleukin-5 promote eosinophil production, survival, and tissue infiltration; eosinophil granule proteins cause direct tissue and endothelial damage, particularly in the heart, lungs, nerves, skin, and gut. In a subset, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (typically anti-myeloperoxidase) contribute to a neutrophil-mediated necrotising vasculitis, giving rise to glomerulonephritis, purpura, and peripheral neuropathy. The two mechanisms-eosinophilic tissue infiltration and ANCA-associated vasculitis-broadly correspond to the different clinical phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis
Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Polyarteritis nodosa and other systemic vasculitides
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count documenting peripheral eosinophilia and inflammatory markers
ANCA testing with anti-MPO and anti-PR3 specificities
Chest imaging for pulmonary infiltrates and sinus assessment
Cardiac evaluation with ECG, troponin, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI as indicated
Nerve conduction studies for suspected mononeuritis multiplex
Urinalysis and renal function for glomerulonephritis, with tissue biopsy of an affected organ where feasible
redFlags: Cardiac involvement with myocarditis, heart failure, or arrhythmia, the principal cause of mortality
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine
Mononeuritis multiplex or other acute neurologic deficit indicating active vasculitis
Gastrointestinal ischaemia, alveolar haemorrhage, or other organ-threatening manifestations requiring urgent immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: With corticosteroids and, when needed, additional immunosuppression and eosinophil-directed biologics, remission is achievable in most patients, though relapse is common and asthma often persists. Prognosis is worst when there is cardiac, severe gastrointestinal, or renal involvement, which are the main determinants of mortality.
pitfalls: Attributing worsening asthma and eosinophilia to poorly controlled asthma alone and missing evolving vasculitis
Failing to assess the heart in apparently stable patients, given the high mortality of cardiac disease
Overlooking mononeuritis multiplex as a marker of active organ-threatening vasculitis
Confusing EGPA with hypereosinophilic syndrome or other eosinophilic lung disease without appropriate ANCA testing and biopsy
management: Systemic corticosteroids as the cornerstone of treatment to induce remission
Add cyclophosphamide or rituximab for organ-threatening vasculitis affecting the heart, kidneys, nerves or gut
Anti-IL-5 biologic mepolizumab for relapsing or refractory non-organ-threatening disease, to reduce steroid dependence and control asthma
Maintenance immunosuppression with azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab after remission is achieved
Optimise control of the underlying asthma and rhinosinusitis with inhaled therapy
Cardiac assessment and treatment of eosinophilic myocarditis and heart failure, with plasma exchange and renal support for severe glomerulonephritis
Multidisciplinary care spanning immunology or rheumatology, cardiology, nephrology, neurology and respiratory medicine, with monitoring for relapse and organ damage
